Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Five years ago, Rohan’s eight-year-old son collapsed on the soccer field and was rushed to the emergency department. The night unfolded in sharp, clinical strokes. Rohan stood just beyond the swinging doors, watching as nurses secured central lines and threaded IV drips into his son’s small arms. The air in the bay was thick with antiseptic, the monitors hummed with relentless urgency, and his son’s chest moved with the mechanical rhythm of a ventilator. His son survived, but the landscape of Rohan’s daily life shifted in the months that followed. Memories of the hospital arrived without warning. A flicker of fluorescent light in a grocery aisle could instantly lock his vision into the image of an empty drip chamber, followed by a sudden wave of sensation—the cold weight of a gown, the sharp beep of a cardiac monitor, the taste of copper in his mouth. The recollection felt completely real, pressing against him from every direction at once. Alongside these intrusions, his body reacted with a jolt of physical reactivity whenever a reminder surfaced. His shoulders tightened, his breath shallowed, and a heavy sweep of negative emotions—fear, horror, and a quiet, persistent shame—settled over him. He found himself lying awake in bed, not because sleep evaded him, but because he chose to stay alert, sitting upright in the hallway chair with a flashlight beside him, convinced that drifting off would leave him unprepared for any sudden crisis. Over weeks, a pattern of avoidance took root. Rohan began rerouting his morning drives to bypass the pediatric wing of the regional hospital. When his wife asked him to attend a neighborhood barbecue where children his son’s age would be playing, he declined, citing exhaustion. In reality, the sight of children laughing in a yard made his chest constrict, and he found himself stepping back into the shadows of the porch. His work as a bomb disposal technician required constant situational awareness. In the decon van’s narrow cabin, the sight of a colleague’s clipboard resting against a box of medical supplies—the outline of a hypodermic needle visible through the packaging—triggered a sharp physical lurch. His hands, usually steady under pressure, trembled. He had to step out into the cool morning air, forcing his breathing to slow before he could resume the call. His shift supervisor had recently noted a hesitation in his response times, and at home, he had withdrawn, flinching when his wife touched his arm, certain that he could not shield his family from the things that might still go wrong. He had come to believe he was a weak person for unraveling under the weight of his own reactions. What frightened him most was the certainty that his body’s alarms meant he was going crazy. He felt trapped in a cycle where he could not stop bad things from happening, only brace for them. The sleepless nights, the sudden flashbacks, the rerouted drives, and the quiet distance between him and his wife had accumulated until the burden became too heavy to carry alone. He sat in a clinician’s office this past week because the exhaustion was beginning to cloud his judgment, and he could no longer ignore the way his own mind had become a site of constant alert. He was afraid he was losing control entirely, but he hoped, quietly, to find a way to sit in a room without bracing for impact, to walk past a clinic without his throat closing, and to believe, however faintly, that he had done what was necessary.
